## apply_patch | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/apply-patch.txt | 2151 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Use `apply_patch` for localized source edits and related multi-file changes. Put the exact patch envelope in `patchText`. Call this tool directly; never invoke `apply_patch` through `shell` or wrap it in a shell heredoc.

Selection:
- Prefer this tool over a full-file rewrite for existing hand-edited files.
- Do not use it for generated files or bulk mechanical rewrites; run the owning generator, formatter, or narrowly scoped transformation instead.
- Use `write` only for a new file best expressed as complete content or an intentional full replacement after reading the current file.
- `git apply` is a shell fallback only for an already-supplied standard unified diff whose provenance and target paths you understand. Read every affected existing file and run `git apply --check` before the real command. Freshness comes from current file bytes and patch context, not Git metadata.

Recovery:
- All sections are parsed and verified before the first filesystem change. If a hunk header or context no longer matches, read the affected file and retry with a smaller patch using fresh, unique context.
- Do not resend the same patch after a verification failure.
- If `git apply --check` or `git apply` fails, stop and re-read every affected file. Translate the smallest still-required change to native `apply_patch` or structured `edit` when exposed; do not mechanically retry the failed diff.
- Do not add `--3way` or `--reject` as automatic recovery, because they can change merge semantics or leave partial artifacts. Never use `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --` to make a patch fit.
- If the result is `uncertain`, some paths may already have changed. Inspect every reported path before retrying; never replay the patch mechanically.

Format:
- Start with `*** Begin Patch`, end with `*** End Patch`, and include one or more file sections.
- Start each section with `*** Add File: <path>`, `*** Delete File: <path>`, or `*** Update File: <path>`.
- An update may include `*** Move to: <path>` and uses `@@` hunks with context, removed (`-`), and added (`+`) lines.
- Every initial-content line in an Add File section must start with `+`.
>>>

## shell | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/shell.txt | 5696 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Executes a command with the configured shell. Commands are parsed with tree-sitter before execution so each constituent command is permission-checked independently. A deterministic destructive-command gate runs before every foreground or background spawn. Under approval-bearing permission modes, confirmable operations such as replacing an existing redirect target require fresh human approval; `allow_all` skips that ask, while catastrophic targets remain hard-denied in every mode. Local Git history rewrites (`commit --amend`, a new `rebase`, or forced tag movement) additionally require `expectedGitHead` containing the exact full object id returned by an immediately preceding `git rev-parse HEAD`; execution fails before spawning if HEAD changed. Select that repository with `workdir`: repository-changing Git global options or environment variables are refused for a rewrite. Published history may only be rewritten with an explicit atomic lease such as `--force-with-lease=refs/heads/main:<expected-full-oid>`; bare `--force`, an implicit lease, and `+` refspecs are refused. Creating a new static file in the OS temp directory does not require approval. For one-off scripts, prefer interpreter stdin such as `python3 - <<'PY'` over fixed `/tmp` filenames. Set `backgroundPurpose: "remoteObserver"` when a command only watches work owned by a remote system, such as a CI run or release. Its terminal process state is a durable wake signal, not proof that the remote work succeeded; after wake, inspect output and re-query the authoritative remote state by stable identifier. A pipeline's exit code is meaningless unless pipefail is in effect: `cargo test | tail -5` exits zero when the tests fail, because only `tail` decides it. `exitPolicy` defaults to `"pipefail"`, so a failure at any stage of a pipeline is the command's failure; `exitPolicy: "all"` also stops at the first failing command in a sequence, and `exitPolicy: "last"` is the way to run a command that is meant to tolerate a failing stage. Every result carries a verification receipt stating whether its exit status covers the whole command; PowerShell has no pipefail equivalent, so only `"all"` is authoritative there. The receipt is downgraded to derived when the command's own text takes the guarantee back: `|| true` or any fallback that cannot fail, `set +e` or `set +o pipefail`, a script handed to an inner `bash -c` or heredoc, and under `"pipefail"` a sequence of statements where only the last one decides the status. Only an authoritative receipt can close a goal success criterion, so run one command, chain with `&&`, or pass `exitPolicy: "all"` when the status has to mean something. Every result reports requested and effective sandbox authority, backend, network policy, resolution kind, and any fallback reason. `read-only` and `workspace-write` require a proved OS confinement backend and fail closed by default. A trusted `sandbox.onUnavailable: "run-unconfined"` policy may run a `workspace-write` request with host authority only for a typed platform, launcher-absence, or namespace-availability failure; it never applies to read-only Agents, untrusted launchers, invalid policy or paths, helper/internal failures, or command execution errors. This fallback preserves the configured permission mode, explicit denies, catastrophic-command refusals, background lifecycle, timeout, and cancellation, but requested filesystem and network restrictions are not OS-enforced. `danger-full-access` is a separate explicit trusted choice that skips restricted-backend discovery and runs as the Zuno user with host filesystem, process, credential, and network access. Explicit permission denies, history-rewrite guards, and catastrophic Shell denials remain terminal. Use workdir instead of changing directories inside the command.

With `background: false` (the default), an attention deadline yields a resumable foreground handle. If waiting is the only useful next action, stay foreground; expected duration or task count alone is not a reason to detach. `backgroundPurpose: "remoteObserver"` describes purpose in either mode and does not require `background: true`. The same command, task ID, original work cycle, hard ceiling, sandbox authority and cancellation contract remain in effect. Serial critical-path waits, including CI needed by the current step, stay foreground: continue the SAME task ID with `bg` wait/output and do not create another observer agent or rerun the command. Each observation is bounded to 60 seconds; an observation timeout is not command completion. Keep polling bounded and honor steering or interruption between waits. Only explicit `background: true` detaches work and enables its normal completion callback; reserve it for independent parallel work or an explicit user request. A foreground handle never schedules that callback. A remoteObserver exit in either mode still requires an authoritative remote-state recheck by stable identifier. A lost process or handle leaves an uncertain outcome; inspect authoritative state before any replay of side effects.

For source changes, prefer native `apply_patch` or structured `edit`, which validate current file bytes or context and report a structured diff. Use `git apply` only for an already-supplied standard unified diff whose provenance and paths you understand: read every affected existing file, run `git apply --check`, and apply it only when that preflight succeeds. Git is not a stale-read or rollback authority. If the check or apply fails, stop, re-read current files, and use a smaller native patch/edit. Do not automatically add `--3way` or `--reject`; never recover with `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --`.
>>>

## goal_propose | crates/zuno-goal/src/description/create-goal.txt | 1261 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Create a durable goal only when explicitly requested by the user or higher-priority instructions. Do not infer a goal from ordinary work. Preserve the requested objective without narrowing it. success_criteria is required: name at least one concrete check that decides whether the objective is met, stated as the check itself rather than as the outcome you hope for. Blank entries are not criteria, and the list is immutable to the model after creation, so a proposal with nothing to check is refused rather than accepted as a question. The result assigns each criterion a short id, such as c1, to cite later. Completing the goal closes every criterion you recorded: name each one in goal_update, either with the receipt id printed by the tool result that verified it or with the reason it will not be verified. An unfinished goal cannot be replaced. Set token_budget only when the user explicitly requested a positive budget.

Creation requires the immutable host context for the current cycle and actual engine turn. The Goal, its criteria, cycle ownership and turn binding commit together, so the same turn can subsequently use goal_update. An old, stopped or already-settled turn cannot create a Goal; creation never resumes or replaces an unfinished Goal.
>>>

## edit | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/edit.txt | 1411 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Applies one or more exact string replacements to a file atomically.

Usage:
- Read this exact file before editing it. Zuno tracks a content digest for the current session and rejects stale edits after an external change.
- The stale-read guard compares the exact bytes recorded by `read`; it does not depend on a Git repository, index, or status.
- Put ordered operations in `edits`. Each operation sees the result of the preceding operation; if any operation fails, nothing is written.
- When editing text from Read tool output, preserve the exact indentation after the line number prefix and never include the prefix in oldString or newString.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit fails if oldString is absent or non-unique unless replaceAll is true.
- Use replaceAll for replacing and renaming strings across the file.
- After a failed native patch or `git apply`, re-read the file before translating the smallest still-required change into exact edit operations. Never use `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --` to make stale text match.
Example:
{"filePath":"/workspace/src/lib.rs","edits":[
  {"oldString":"fn old_name()","newString":"fn new_name()"},
  {"oldString":"old_name()","newString":"new_name()","replaceAll":true}
]}
>>>

## glob | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/glob.txt | 516 bytes | trailing-newline: no
<<<
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open-ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Task tool instead
- You have the capability to call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively perform multiple searches as a batch that are potentially useful.
>>>

## grep | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/grep.txt | 658 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
- Fast content search tool that works with any codebase size
- Searches file contents using regular expressions
- Supports full regex syntax (eg. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+", etc.)
- Filter files by pattern with the include parameter (eg. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}")
- Returns file paths and line numbers with matching lines
- Use this tool when you need to find files containing specific patterns
- If you need to identify/count the number of matches within files, use the shell tool with `rg` (ripgrep) directly. Do NOT use `grep`.
- When you are doing an open-ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Task tool instead
>>>

## question | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/question.txt | 1403 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Ask for a material user decision that cannot be discovered from available evidence.
In Plan this is a clarification. In ordinary Work this registers required human input
and suspends automatic execution until the exact request is answered.
For an optional question that should not delay independent work or your final summary,
use question_async instead.

Usage notes:
- Ask only when the answer materially changes the outcome and cannot be discovered from available evidence
- Defer non-blocking choices and do not ask for reassurance
- Prefer one concise question and ask no more than three at once
- When `custom` is enabled (default), a "Type your own answer" option is added automatically; don't include "Other" or catch-all options
- Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive options; set `multiple: true` only when combinations are meaningful
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label
- The request persists independently of this tool call; the user may answer later or choose Defer
- Tool results are receipts. Actual answers arrive through the durable session inbox once
- A partial or empty answer leaves the unanswered items pending and is never approval
- Cancellation is a refusal, not an answer; do not fabricate a selection
- To request authorization of an exact Plan for Work, use plan_exit, not a generic question
>>>

## read | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/read.txt | 1083 bytes | trailing-newline: no
<<<
Read a file or directory from the local filesystem. If the path does not exist, an error is returned.

Usage:
- The filePath parameter should be an absolute path.
- By default, this tool returns up to 2000 lines from the start of the file.
- The offset parameter is the line number to start from (1-indexed).
- To read later sections, call this tool again with a larger offset.
- Use the grep tool to find specific content in large files or files with long lines.
- If you are unsure of the correct file path, use the glob tool to look up filenames by glob pattern.
- Contents are returned with each line prefixed by its line number as `<line>: <content>`. For directories, entries are returned one per line (without line numbers) with a trailing `/` for subdirectories.
- Any line longer than 2000 characters is truncated.
- Call this tool in parallel when you know there are multiple files you want to read.
- Avoid tiny repeated slices (30 line chunks). If you need more context, read a larger window.
- This tool can read image files and PDFs and return them as file attachments.
>>>

## report_write | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/report-write.txt | 881 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Save a research report, audit, inventory, or other text deliverable as a host-managed file.
Available independently of source editing: a read-only investigator can publish reports without using Shell, write, or apply_patch.

Supply a plain filename (for example audit.md or inventory.txt) and the complete UTF-8 content, up to 1 MiB. The host chooses an immutable path under the worktree's .zuno/reports/ directory and returns its exact path, byte count, and SHA-256. Always cite that returned path; do not invent an output path or claim that another requested destination was written.

This tool cannot edit source files, configuration, extensions, existing reports, or arbitrary destinations. To revise a report, publish its complete new contents in a new call. A parent with suitable edit permission can integrate or copy the returned artifact to another requested destination.
>>>

## task | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/task.txt | 2319 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Delegate a self-contained unit of work to the named child `agent` in its own session.
Every call requires five non-empty top-level strings: `agent`, `objective`, `deliverable`, `instructions`, and `success_evidence`. This also applies when continuing with `task_id`.
`intent` is an optional UI label, not the child's objective, and never replaces `objective`. Do not nest the fields under `contract` or use legacy `prompt`, `description`, `subagent_type`, or `load_skills` arguments.

Minimal valid example:
```json
{
  "agent": "explorer",
  "objective": "Locate the tool argument validation boundary",
  "deliverable": "A short report with file and symbol references",
  "instructions": "Trace argument validation without editing files",
  "success_evidence": "Identify the validation entry point and a matching test"
}
```
Choose `agent` from the currently available delegation targets; keep the same five-field shape for other agents. On validation failure, correct the named arguments using the current schema; do not repeat the unchanged call or invent missing outcomes.
Use `scope.include`/`scope.exclude`, `constraints.must`/`constraints.must_not`, and `dependencies` when they materially bound or enable the work.
The child model, reasoning, MCP, Skill configuration, and sandbox inherit from the parent composition and are narrowed by the selected Agent's policy.
The parent retains integration decisions and final verification. Do not duplicate the delegated work in the parent.
Foreground is the default and waits until the child answers. If waiting for that result is the only useful next action, stay foreground; do not detach just to end the parent turn. Use `background: true` only for independent parallel work or an explicit user request; it returns immediately with a fresh job id.
Background jobs default to `reportDelivery: "nextStep"`, which adds the terminal report to the parent's next step and wakes it. Use `"quiet"` only when the persisted job result will be inspected separately.
Pass `task_id` from a previous call to continue that same child session instead of starting a fresh one.
Skills are not task arguments; the child can load only skills exposed by its effective Agent capabilities.
Do not create overlapping children unless their `scope` ownership is explicit and non-overlapping.
>>>

This tool is read-only and safe to call in parallel with other read-only tools.

## plan_update | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/plan-update.txt | 2416 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Create or mutate the durable plan for the current session with one tagged operation.
Call plan_get immediately before every plan_update and copy its returned revision into expected_revision. The only exception is action=create after plan_get returned null; only that first-plan case may omit expected_revision. Never guess, reuse an older revision, or omit it merely because the intended change is small.
Use action=create to create the first strategic plan, or to replace the visible root for a genuinely new objective. Supply a title and one or more steps; the host generates stable step ids. Replacing an existing plan requires its current expected_revision.
Use action=patch to change only the plan title or named steps. Each step patch carries the id returned by plan_get and may change its title, status, or both.
Use action=append to add one or more new steps. The host generates their ids; never invent or resend ids for appended steps.
Use action=push when one active step needs a focused temporary subplan. It atomically suspends the current plan and creates the visible child plan with host-generated step ids.
Use action=pop only after every child step is terminal. Pop carries only expected_revision; it atomically archives the child and restores the exact suspended parent.
Every operation that changes an existing plan requires expected_revision equal to the revision returned by plan_get. A stale revision is rejected without changing the plan.
Pending steps require exactly one in_progress step. Completed and superseded steps are terminal and cannot regress. A fully terminal plan has no in_progress step.
If a commit, build, tag, deployment, or other verification input changes after a completed gate, append a new artifact-scoped verification step; never reuse or regress the old completed gate.
Do not complete or supersede a step while a linked Job is queued, running, uncertain, or still has an unconsumed report. Reconcile its durable result first.
Update the plan immediately when a step starts, completes, is superseded, or changes scope. Before a final answer, reconcile the active step so durable state never relies on prose to communicate progress.
Link a newly-created plan to the active goal with goal_id when one exists. Do not rewrite the user's goal or success criteria through this tool.
This tool changes durable state and is never replayed implicitly after an uncertain failure.
>>>

Atomically add, update, or remove durable work items for the current session.

When one atomic batch adds dependent items, assign explicit stable ids to every newly added item before referencing them from parent_id or dependencies; never invent positional ids such as todo_1. Preserve an existing id instead of deleting and recreating an item.

## goal_update | crates/zuno-goal/src/description/update-goal.txt | 2419 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Read the current goal before changing it and pass its revision as expected_revision. If the revision is stale, read again instead of overwriting concurrent work. `status: in_progress` (or `active`) is only an idempotent confirmation that an already-active Goal is still running; it does not resume a paused or blocked Goal, which requires the user to run `/goal resume`. Model completion cannot close a paused Goal through an independent request; the user can explicitly request native `/goal complete` without resuming it. An optional intent records why the call was attempted. Mark the Goal complete only when authoritative evidence proves every requirement and no required work remains. A user-created Goal with an empty declaration and empty criterion ledger has no implicit checklist, even after changing files; ownership, unfinished work, capability and safety checks still apply. For a declared checklist, close each success criterion in the same call: name it in satisfy_criteria with the receipt id printed by the tool result that verified it, or in waive_criteria with the reason it will not be verified. A goal cannot complete while any declared criterion is still open, and a missing or inconsistent ledger is a contract error. Any edit after a criterion was satisfied invalidates the evidence for it, and the edits the tools report also reopen the criterion, so never read a criterion that stayed closed as still proven: run the check again after your last change and cite the new receipt. Report blocked with a concrete blocking_condition as soon as a true impasse prevents meaningful progress. This stages an observation; the returned Goal remains in its actual state. The host counts completed Goal turns and applies blocked after three matching turns. Do not count three turns yourself before reporting. Repeated calls within one turn do not increase the count; progress or a different condition resets it. Do not use this tool merely because a turn is ending, work is difficult, the budget is low, or more verification remains.

Completion also requires the current native Goal/cycle/actual-turn binding and immutable host snapshot. A fresh expected_revision does not grant authority over an old or unowned Goal, including a blocked Goal left behind by an independent request. Scope checks, criterion changes and completion are atomic; a stale turn cannot waive criteria or complete a different Goal.

## capability_claim | crates/zuno-goal/src/description/capability-claim.txt | 1212 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Record what this session believes an external capability can do and how it knows, before configuration that relies on it is written. capability names the feature, such as bedrock:converse:structured_output; subject names what it is claimed about, such as a model id. state is the provenance, not the truth value: documented requires at least one entry in sources naming the vendor document for this exact subject (a URL, a title or a file path); probed requires probeReceiptId, the receipt id printed by the tool result whose request exercised the capability and whose response was observed; inferred means it was concluded from something else, such as a sibling model's documentation; unknown means it has not been checked. Only documented or probed claims may be relied on, and a goal that changes the workspace cannot complete while an inferred or unknown claim recorded under it stands. A write to the workspace retires an earlier probe, so probe again after the last change and record the claim again. Recording the same capability and subject again replaces the earlier claim; record a weaker state when new information retracts one. Never record documented without a citation or probed without a receipt.
>>>

## webfetch | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/webfetch.txt | 749 bytes | trailing-newline: no
<<<
- Fetches content from a specified URL
- Takes a URL and optional format as input
- Fetches the URL content, converts to requested format (markdown by default)
- Returns the content in the specified format
- Use this tool when you need to retrieve and analyze web content

Usage notes:
  - IMPORTANT: if another tool is present that offers better web fetching capabilities, is more targeted to the task, or has fewer restrictions, prefer using that tool instead of this one.
  - The URL must be a fully-formed valid URL
  - HTTP URLs will be automatically upgraded to HTTPS
  - Format options: "markdown" (default), "text", or "html"
  - This tool is read-only and does not modify any files
  - Results may be summarized if the content is very large
>>>

## write | crates/zuno-tools/src/description/write.txt | 1158 bytes | trailing-newline: yes
<<<
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- Only `filePath` and `content` are required.
- If this is an existing file, read that exact file first. Zuno tracks its content digest for the current session and rejects stale writes after an external change.
- The stale-read guard compares the exact bytes recorded by `read`; it does not depend on a Git repository, index, or status.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.
- Do not use a full-file write as a blind fallback after native patch or `git apply` failure; re-read first and replace the whole file only when that replacement is intentional. Never use `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --` to manufacture the expected pre-image.
Example: {"filePath":"/workspace/new.txt","content":"complete file contents\n"}
>>>
